Digital life

Do social media make us unhappy?

The average effect is small, but it is not the same for everyone. How you use them matters more than how long.

Few questions spark as much debate. Some blame social media for rising anxiety and depression among teenagers; others say the panic is overblown. What do we know?

What studies say

In 2019, Amy Orben and Andrew Przybylski analysed data from more than 350,000 teenagers. The link between digital technology use and wellbeing was negative but very small, comparable to that of wearing glasses or eating potatoes regularly. Other researchers, such as Jonathan Haidt, argue that the effect is larger in teenage girls and with heavy use, and the debate is still open.

Experiments add something more. In 2020, Hunt Allcott and colleagues paid adult Facebook users to deactivate their accounts for four weeks. Those who did had a small improvement in wellbeing, spent more time watching TV and with friends, and used Facebook less afterwards.

Not just how much, but how

What seems to do most harm is social comparison with retouched lives, passive endless scrolling, use that eats into sleep and experiences of harassment. On the other hand, using social media to keep in touch with friends or find community can be positive.

Constant comparison

Social media mostly shows other people's best moments and best photos. Jasmine Fardouly and colleagues found that after spending ten minutes on Facebook, young women prone to comparing their appearance with others felt worse about how they looked than after browsing a neutral website. Remembering that what you see is a selection, and unfollowing accounts that make you feel bad, are simple steps that help.

What lies behind the association

An analysis by Yvonne Kelly of data from more than 10,000 British adolescents found that heavy social media use was associated with more depressive symptoms, especially in girls. Much of that link was explained by three factors: poorer sleep, online harassment and lower self-esteem and body image. So rather than counting minutes, it makes sense to protect sleep, for example by keeping phones out of the bedroom, and to watch out for harassment.

What usually helps

  • Notice how you feel after using each app.
  • Unfollow accounts that make you feel worse.
  • Take your phone out of the bedroom at night.
  • Use social media actively: talk to people rather than just watching.
  • Try a break of a few days and see what changes.

References

  1. Orben, A. y Przybylski, A. K. (2019). The association between adolescent well-being and digital technology use. Nature Human Behaviour, 3(2), 173–182.
  2. Allcott, H. et al. (2020). The welfare effects of social media. American Economic Review, 110(3), 629–676.
  3. Fardouly, J., Diedrichs, P. C., Vartanian, L. R. y Halliwell, E. (2015). Social comparisons on social media: the impact of Facebook on young women's body image concerns and mood. Body Image, 13, 38–45.
  4. Kelly, Y., Zilanawala, A., Booker, C. y Sacker, A. (2018). Social media use and adolescent mental health: findings from the UK Millennium Cohort Study. EClinicalMedicine, 6, 59–68.
